script: [serious] In March 1918, one of the largest ships in the United States Navy sailed out of Barbados, bound for Baltimore. She was more than five hundred and forty feet long. She was carrying around ten thousand tons of ore. And she had hundreds of people aboard, three hundred and six by the Navy's usual count. She was due in Baltimore nine days later. She never arrived. There was no distress call. No lifeboat was ever found. No wreckage. No bodies. More than a century later, the U.S.S. Cyclops is still one of the largest losses of life in U.S. Navy history not directly involving combat. And nobody knows what happened to her. This is the story of her last voyage. The cargo she was carrying, the engine that was already broken, the captain her own crew feared, and the theories that have tried, and failed, to explain how a ship that size could simply disappear. The Cyclops was not a warship. She was a collier, a floating coal depot, built in Philadelphia and launched in 1910. Her job was to carry fuel to the fleet. Huge steel towers rose along her deck, part of the machinery that loaded and unloaded coal at sea. She was built to carry around eight thousand tons in normal service, and up to around ten thousand eight hundred tons at most. For years she supplied American warships, from the Baltic to the Caribbean. In 1914, during the American occupation of Veracruz in Mexico, she fuelled the patrol ships offshore and helped evacuate refugees, work that earned her the thanks of the State Department. She was a workhorse. Big, slow, reliable, and almost never in the headlines. In 1917, when the United States entered the First World War, she was formally commissioned into the Navy, with a Navy crew. That June she crossed the Atlantic in a convoy to Saint-Nazaire in France, carrying supplies for the war. By the start of 1918, she was part of the Naval Overseas Transportation Service, the Navy's wartime cargo fleet. In January 1918, she sailed south with a load of coal for British warships operating off South America. Her final assignment looked simple. Deliver the coal, pick up a cargo in Brazil, and bring it home. The cargo was manganese ore. Manganese was essential for making steel, and America needed steel for the war. At Rio de Janeiro, the Cyclops was loaded with around ten thousand eight hundred tons of it, right up to her maximum, and possibly beyond. Manganese ore is extraordinarily dense. A full load sits low and heavy in the hull. There was another problem. Before leaving Rio, her captain reported a cracked cylinder in the starboard engine. That engine was out of action. The ship would have to cross thousands of miles of ocean on one engine. A survey board looked at the damage and recommended she return to the United States for repairs. So she did. She left Rio in mid February, called at Salvador in Brazil, and headed north for Baltimore. Running on one shaft, she was limited to around ten knots. It would be a long, slow trip home, through waters where German submarines and raiders were hunting Allied ships. But on the third of March, she made a stop that wasn't on her schedule. Barbados. According to reports, she was sitting so low that the water was above her load line. On the fourth of March, she sailed again. That was the last time anyone is known to have seen her. Her commander was George Worley. And the more investigators learned about him, the stranger the story became. Worley had been born in Germany, under a different name, Johan Frederick Wichmann. He had come to America by jumping ship in San Francisco as a teenager, and later ran a saloon on the city's Barbary Coast. In 1917 he was commissioned into the naval reserve. His crew did not like him. Former sailors described him as abusive and violent. One story claimed he once chased an officer with a pistol. Another said he would walk the deck in long underwear and a derby hat. And in the middle of a war against Germany, there were whispers that he was pro-German. A U.S. consul in Barbados sent a telegram after the ship had disappeared. It reported that the engines were in very poor condition, and noted that many Germanic names appeared among the crew. It passed on unconfirmed rumors of trouble aboard. And it ended with a line that still sends a chill. I fear fate worse than sinking, the consul wrote, though possibly based on instinctive dislike felt towards master. None of it was ever proven. But it made people ask a question. Had the Cyclops been betrayed by her own captain? The Cyclops was due in Baltimore around the thirteenth of March. When she didn't appear, the Navy did not announce it straight away. A ship running on one engine might simply be slow. Ships and stations were asked to look out for her. Nothing. A rumor spread that a tanker had seen her off Virginia on the ninth of March. The tanker's captain denied it. In April 1918, the disappearance became front-page news across the country. A ship that big, with that many people, could not just vanish. And yet she had. On the first of June 1918, the Navy, through Assistant Secretary Franklin Roosevelt, declared the Cyclops officially lost with all hands. The Navy's own investigation later admitted defeat. Many theories have been advanced, it said, but none that satisfactorily accounts for her disappearance. Among the people lost was a passenger, Alfred Gottschalk, America's consul general in Rio de Janeiro, heading home. Even the number of people lost has never been settled. The Navy's usual figure is three hundred and six, but newspapers at the time printed other numbers, and the records disagree. The families of everyone aboard never received an answer. No funerals with coffins. No graves. Just a name on a list, and a ship that never came home. So what happened to the Cyclops? The first suspect was the enemy. Germany was sinking ships across the Atlantic. But after the war, German records showed no claim to have sunk her. Then there was Worley. Sabotage, or a mutiny. But there was never any evidence. The Bermuda Triangle has been blamed too. But that idea came decades later, and researchers have found nothing to support it. The more likely answer is less dramatic, and more frightening. On the tenth of March, a violent storm hit the coast off Virginia. The Navy's historians say she probably sank in an unexpected storm. Picture the ship that night. One engine. Loaded to the limit with dense ore. Some experts think the ore could shift, or that water got in and slowly destroyed her stability. In a 2009 documentary, an expert from Lloyd's of London suggested that wet manganese ore can behave almost like a slurry, sliding to one side and making a ship list. Others think her long hull simply broke under the strain. One retired admiral argued that her steel beams had eroded over the years, and that big waves could have put enormous stress on the middle of the ship until it gave way. If any of that happened fast enough, there would be no time to send a message. And here is the detail that keeps the mystery alive. The Cyclops had sister ships. In 1941, two of them, the Proteus and the Nereus, by then sold as merchant ships and both loaded with bauxite ore, also vanished without a trace in the Atlantic. Same design. Same kind of cargo. Same silence. So was it a storm, a design flaw, or something we still don't understand? Tell me in the comments. This is Dossier Decoded.
